questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a political culture measure captures.
questions.stem: A researcher plots a country's survey responses on a scatter chart. Which reading treats political culture correctly?

options.text: Political culture is read from the pattern of shared beliefs and expectations the chart summarises
Political culture is the percentage of voters who say they are loyal to the state
options.misconception: confuses political culture with one single opinion about the state

options.text: Political culture is identical to the country's income per person and its growth rate
options.misconception: equates political culture with material economic indicators

options.text: Political culture is whatever the chart shows about a single election result
options.misconception: treats one election result as a measure of culture

questions.explanation: Political culture concerns shared orientations and expectations about political life, so survey response patterns can evidence it. It is not one question, an economic measure or a single election result.
questions.hint: Look for shared expectations, not one statistic.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Label participant and observer cultures from a chart.

stimulus.body: The chart plots two lines from 1990 to 2020. The upper line rises from 30 to 58 per cent and is labelled 'citizens who vote, join associations and follow debates'. The lower line falls from 52 to 34 per cent and is labelled 'citizens who follow politics at a distance without taking part'.

questions.stem: Reading the chart, how should the two lines be labelled in political culture terms?

options.text: The upper line measures political efficacy and the lower line political indifference
options.misconception: confuses participation with a sense of political efficacy

options.text: The upper line is a participant culture and the lower line an observer culture
The upper line shows liberal culture and the lower line authoritarian culture
options.misconception: reads voting levels as evidence of a liberal or authoritarian culture

options.text: Both lines measure participant cultures that differ only in the strength of feeling
options.misconception: assumes any attention to politics counts as participation

questions.explanation: The rising line combines voting, association membership and debate, the signature of a participant culture; the falling line shows citizens who observe without joining in. Interest alone is not participation.
questions.hint: Separate taking part from following along.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish political values from political attitudes.
questions.stem: Explain the difference between a political value and a political attitude, and show how the same person can hold a value and an attitude that point in opposite directions.

answer.exemplar: A value is a deep and relatively stable conviction about what is good or desirable in political life, such as holding that equal treatment before the law matters more than state security. An attitude is a more specific and less stable judgement about a particular object or policy. The same person can value equal legal protection strongly while holding a negative attitude towards a specific law they believe weakens it, because the value sets the standard and the attitude applies it to a concrete case.

questions.explanation: Values set the standard while attitudes apply it to particular policies. They can diverge because a strong value may lead someone to oppose a concrete measure they think violates it.
questions.hint: One sets the standard; the other judges a case.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify socialisation through a non-family agent.

stimulus.body: In a group interview, one participant said she learned to vote from her grandmother, another said he started paying attention to politics after a workplace dispute over shift allocation, and a third said she has never voted but watches the news each evening because her employer encourages debate about public spending.

questions.stem: Which participant's account best illustrates political socialisation through an agent other than the family?

options.text: The first participant, who names her grandmother as the source of the habit
options.misconception: treats the family as the only source of political learning

options.text: The third participant, who follows the evening news out of personal interest
options.misconception: assumes self-directed news viewing counts as socialisation by an agent

options.text: The third participant, who reports political discussion being encouraged at work
The first participant, who describes a workplace dispute over shift allocation
options.misconception: reads a workplace dispute as the worker's family socialising them

questions.explanation: The third participant describes an outside influence, an employer, prompting political discussion, which is socialisation by a non-family agent. Family influence and self-chosen news watching are different processes.
questions.hint: Ask who prompted the political attention.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a chart of socialising agents cautiously.
questions.stem: A chart lists four agents with the same width of bars: school, family, media and peers. Which reading of the equal bars is most defensible?

options.text: The agents are equally influential because the bar widths are identical
options.misconception: reads identical bar lengths as proof of identical influence

options.text: The chart proves that no agent matters more than any other in practice
options.misconception: treats the absence of differences as proof of practical equality

options.text: The chart shows that influence depends on the age of the person being socialised
options.misconception: invents an age dimension that the chart never records

options.text: Equal bar widths show only that the survey used the same scale for each agent

questions.explanation: Equal bar widths only show that each agent was measured on the same scale; they say nothing about relative influence, and identical readings never prove practical equality. No age dimension is recorded.
questions.hint: Ask what the chart actually plots.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what media influence depends on.
questions.stem: A graph shows radio listening peaks at 6am and 7pm and television viewing peaks at 9pm. What does the media's contribution to political socialisation depend on?

options.text: On what audiences take from broadcasts, not on how many hours are broadcast
On the total number of hours of political content produced each year
options.misconception: confuses volume of output with the effect on audiences

options.text: On the proportion of broadcasts that cover political topics at all
options.misconception: assumes coverage volume determines what audiences take from it

options.text: On the number of separate channels carrying political discussion daily
options.misconception: believes channel counts measure the strength of socialising influence

questions.explanation: Exposure is only an opportunity to socialise; what audiences take from broadcasts is what shapes political orientations. Hours produced, topic coverage and channel counts describe supply, not effect.
questions.hint: Supply of broadcasts is not the same as effect.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a political system from a regime.

stimulus.body: Card one: regular multi-party elections are held on schedule; the legislature is elected; the executive is drawn from the legislature; courts sit independently. Card two: the same country has never held a referendum, the only opposition newspaper was closed two years ago, and the head of the state security service is a close relative of the president.

questions.stem: Using the two cards, which distinction is correctly drawn?

options.text: The two cards show the same country at two moments in a single reform process
options.misconception: reads two different descriptors as stages of one reform

options.text: The first card describes a system, while the second describes features of a regime
The first card describes a regime, while the second describes features of a system
options.misconception: swaps the two terms that the cards are meant to separate

options.text: The two cards together show that the country is a stable hybrid regime
options.misconception: jumps to a single classification without weighing the features

questions.explanation: A system is the durable institutional arrangement of rules; a regime is the practical pattern of power exercised within it. The first card lists institutions, the second lists how power behaves.
questions.hint: One card lists rules, the other lists behaviour.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how opposition and media suppression reinforce each other.
questions.stem: Explain how the absence of meaningful opposition and the absence of free media contribute to an authoritarian regime, and why the two reinforce each other.

answer.exemplar: Without a meaningful opposition, the executive faces no organised alternative that could take office, so elections confirm existing power rather than allowing it to be transferred. Without free media, the government can shape what citizens hear, suppress reporting on its own conduct and portray opponents as dangerous, so citizens cannot form an informed view of who deserves support. The two conditions reinforce each other because a party with no platform can win only if the public is not given a reason to prefer another.

questions.explanation: Absence of opposition removes the chance that power can change hands, and control of the media removes the information citizens would need to demand that change. Each condition strengthens the other.
questions.hint: Ask what each condition removes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a regional spread within a single national survey.

stimulus.body: The survey asked 1,200 adults whether they agreed with the statement that most people can be trusted, and recorded the share in each of twelve regions. The chart shows the regional spread from 18 per cent to 71 per cent, and the note states that all twelve regions were sampled with the same wording and timing.

questions.stem: On the basis of the note, what does the regional spread in the chart indicate?

options.text: That some regions have a culture of trust while others have none at all
options.misconception: reads regional differences as wholly different national cultures

options.text: That the twelve regions belong to different political cultures entirely
options.misconception: assumes each region is a separate political culture

options.text: That trust is unevenly distributed across regions without implying different nations
That the survey's wording must have been changed between regions
options.misconception: suggests inconsistent wording without any evidence for it

questions.explanation: The chart shows trust varying within one country, a regional pattern rather than a comparison of national political cultures. Identical wording and timing across regions rule out a methodological artefact.
questions.hint: One country, several regions, one survey.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess a claim that falling turnout proves political apathy.
questions.stem: Judge this reading: 'Where turnout fell, political culture must have become apathetic.' Which assessment of the chart and the claim fits?

options.text: The claim holds, because turnout is the only measure of political culture
options.misconception: treats turnout as a complete measure of political culture

options.text: The claim holds, because a culture of observation always precedes apathy
options.misconception: assumes low turnout always demonstrates a settled loss of interest

options.text: The claim fails only if the survey excluded non-voters from the sample
options.misconception: imposes a sampling condition the chart never raises

options.text: The claim fails, because interest without participation is not the same as apathy

questions.explanation: Falling turnout alone cannot distinguish political observation from apathy, because observers may follow debate closely without voting. The claim overreads the chart, and nothing in it suggests a sampling flaw.
questions.hint: Distinguish watching politics from abandoning it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a value may stay steady while attitudes on a policy move.
questions.stem: A chart shows support for a freedom of information law falling from 62 to 38 per cent, while a related value question on openness of government stays near 70 per cent. What does the pair show?

options.text: Support for a specific measure can fall while the underlying value remains strong
The two series must measure the same thing, since one follows the other
options.misconception: assumes the two series measure the same underlying thing

options.text: A steady value score means the policy question was not answered consistently
options.misconception: treats a stable value score as evidence of inconsistent answering

options.text: Values change automatically once attitudes towards a policy move
options.misconception: believes values shift automatically as policy attitudes shift

questions.explanation: The value series records a standing conviction while the policy series records a judgement about one measure, so they can move differently and both stay reliable. People may value openness yet dislike a specific draft.
questions.hint: A value is standing, an attitude is specific.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a cohort chart showing when political interest begins.

stimulus.body: The chart plots the share of each age group who say they first took an interest in politics in their teens, and the share who say they took it up in adulthood. For the youngest group the figures are 18 and 74 per cent; for the oldest group they are 61 and 22 per cent.

questions.stem: What does the chart show about when political orientations tend to be formed?

options.text: That people who become interested in adulthood always abandon their earlier views
options.misconception: assumes later interest means earlier views were discarded

options.text: That the age at which interest begins varies systematically across age groups
That adult political interest is not political socialisation at all
options.misconception: excludes adult-onset interest from the socialisation process

options.text: That every generation forms its political views at exactly the same stage
options.misconception: generalises one cohort's pattern to every cohort

questions.explanation: The chart shows a cohort gradient: the youngest group mostly took up politics in adulthood, the oldest mostly in their teens. That is systematic variation in timing, not later interest erasing earlier views.
questions.hint: Compare the two age groups, not the average.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare family, school and peer agents as socialisers.
questions.stem: Explain how the family, schools and peers differ as political socialising agents, and give one reason each operates differently.

answer.exemplar: The family socialises early, through repeated conversation and example inside the household, and it is the agent whose influence on children is most sustained and hardest to escape. Schools socialise formally and publicly, teaching civic rules and exposing pupils to competing accounts of the political order in a setting the family does not control. Peers socialise horizontally and experimentally, testing views against equals and applying pressure to conform. The three differ in timing, in authority and in the pressure each applies.

questions.explanation: Family agents work early and through sustained personal contact, schools work formally and institutionally, peers work horizontally through conformity pressure. Timing, authority and the type of pressure each applies distinguish them.
questions.hint: Compare timing, authority and pressure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare broadcasting hours with trust in broadcasters.

stimulus.body: The chart compares three measures for each of six countries: hours of political broadcasting per week, the share of the audience who trusts broadcasters, and a survey score for confidence in democratic institutions. In three countries broadcasting hours are high while trust in broadcasters is low; in the other three the two move together.

questions.stem: What does the chart suggest about broadcasting hours and political socialisation?

options.text: Longer broadcasts reliably produce higher trust in the institutions they cover
options.misconception: assumes more exposure automatically raises trust and confidence

options.text: Broadcasting hours have almost no effect once trust in broadcasters is measured
options.misconception: concludes exposure never matters at all

options.text: Hours of exposure matter less than whether audiences trust the source
Trust in broadcasters and confidence in institutions are the same measurement
options.misconception: treats trust in broadcasters as identical to institutional confidence

questions.explanation: The countries where hours are high but trust is low show exposure alone does not deliver socialising influence, because what audiences take from a source depends on whether it is trusted. Trust and confidence are separate measures.
questions.hint: Ask whether the audience believes the source.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a country whose rules are observed in practice differently.
questions.stem: A country holds regular competitive elections and has a written constitution, yet election outcomes are never respected by the outgoing office. How should the chart of features be read?

options.text: The country must be classified as a democracy because elections are held
options.misconception: treats the holding of elections as sufficient for a democratic classification

options.text: The country must be classified as a hybrid regime because some rules exist
options.misconception: applies a single label without weighing the evidence of practice

options.text: The system cannot exist at all when its outcomes are never respected
options.misconception: assumes institutional rules cannot exist without being respected

options.text: The written rules describe a system, while the practice describes an authoritarian regime

questions.explanation: Competitive elections and a written constitution describe institutional design, while ignoring outcomes describes the regime in operation. Holding elections does not make a system democratic when results are never honoured.
questions.hint: Separate the rules on paper from their observance.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify features that mark authoritarian rule.
questions.stem: Which combination of features most clearly indicates authoritarian rule in a regime profile?

options.text: Concentrated power without meaningful opposition and without free expression
A large legislature, regular elections and a multiparty press in good health
options.misconception: lists democratic institutions and calls the profile authoritarian

options.text: Strong parliament, an independent judiciary and a peaceful transfer of office
options.misconception: describes democratic accountability and treats it as a sign of authoritarianism

options.text: A single official party endorsed by the electorate through regular ballots
options.misconception: assumes a single party means the absence of political competition

questions.explanation: Authoritarian rule is marked by power that cannot be challenged through opposition or free expression. A large legislature, a free press, an independent judiciary and a single endorsed party indicate the opposite.
questions.hint: Ask whether power can be challenged.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two culture indicators may diverge.

stimulus.body: Two indicators are compared across the same fifty states. The first is the share of adults who report membership of a political organisation or a voluntary association. The second is the share who report a close friend they discuss politics with. The chart shows the two series moving in opposite directions in eleven states.

questions.stem: According to the method note, what does the divergence between the two series suggest?

options.text: That one of the two indicators has been recorded incorrectly in those states
options.misconception: jumps to a data error without any evidence of one

options.text: That organised activity and political discussion measure different aspects of culture
That states with more discussion must have less organised activity by law
options.misconception: invents a legal constraint that the note never mentions

options.text: That political culture in a state can only be captured by a single indicator
options.misconception: assumes a single indicator can capture a state's political culture

questions.explanation: The two indicators capture different dimensions, formal organisation and informal discussion, so they need not move together within a state. Divergence is expected and does not indicate a recording error.
questions.hint: Different indicators can measure different things.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how attention can be high while participation stays low.
questions.stem: Explain how a country could have a high share of citizens who follow political debate but a low share who participate, and what that combination implies.

answer.exemplar: Debate can be consumed passively, through broadcasts, comment sections and conversations, so attention is cheap while participation requires time, money and risk. A country where many people follow the debate closely but few join parties, campaign, vote or petition therefore shows an observer culture among a large minority. The combination signals that barriers to participation are high even though the information environment is open, and it distinguishes disinterest from exclusion.

questions.explanation: Following debate costs little, while participation demands time, money and some risk, so attention can be high while involvement stays low. The pairing points to high barriers, not absent interest.
questions.hint: Attention is cheap, participation is not.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Show that a shared value can coexist with different votes.

stimulus.body: Three respondents gave the same answer to a value question about whether public office should be contested at elections. The first added that they would vote for whichever candidate their union endorsed. The second said they trust their councillor completely and always vote for them. The third said they would vote against an unpopular incumbent even though they support competitive elections.

questions.stem: What do these quotes together illustrate about values and attitudes?

options.text: That the value question was understood differently by each respondent
options.misconception: assumes different answers mean different understandings of the question

options.text: That stated values have no bearing on how people actually vote
options.misconception: concludes that values are unrelated to voting behaviour

options.text: That a shared value can coexist with sharply different voting attitudes
That only the first respondent's answer reflects a genuine political value
options.misconception: rules out the second and third answers as insincere

questions.explanation: All three endorse competitive elections yet their voting attitudes differ, because a value sets a principle while an attitude applies it to a particular choice. A shared value does not predict a shared vote.
questions.hint: The principle is common; the choices are not.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret rising turnout alongside stable attitudes.
questions.stem: A chart shows turnout rising sharply among young adults over ten years while attitudes on one issue remain stable. Which interpretation is best supported?

options.text: The stable attitudes prove the young adults were not really socialised politically
options.misconception: assumes stable attitudes prove an absence of political learning

options.text: The turnout rise shows that socialisation has replaced the older cohorts
options.misconception: reads rising turnout as the displacement of older voters

options.text: The chart shows that socialisation works only on participation and never on views
options.misconception: limits socialisation to participation and excludes attitude formation

options.text: Socialisation can strengthen how people act without changing what they believe

questions.explanation: Socialisation can affect how actively people engage without shifting the content of their beliefs, so rising turnout with stable attitudes is consistent with it. It shows nothing about replacing older cohorts.
questions.hint: Acting and believing can move separately.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the agent most decisive for first political formation.
questions.stem: Which agent is most likely to be decisive in shaping a first-time voter's early political outlook?

options.text: The family, because political habits are usually formed in the household first
Television, because it reaches the largest audience of first-time voters
options.misconception: assumes audience size determines formative influence

options.text: Trade unions, because organised labour shapes every newcomer's politics
options.misconception: generalises about organised labour's role in every case

options.text: Formal civics teaching, because the curriculum is the earliest common influence
options.misconception: assumes the curriculum has more influence than the household

questions.explanation: The household is the earliest and most persistent setting for forming political habits, so it usually has the first decisive influence. Audience size and curricular reach do not outweigh timing.
questions.hint: Think about the first setting, not the biggest audience.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of surrounding commentary on audiences.

stimulus.body: Presenter: we put the same clip to two groups at the end of the week. Group A saw it on a channel that made no editorial comment; group B saw the identical clip on a channel that had spent the preceding ten minutes criticising the government. Asked afterwards what they thought of the minister, group B's answers were far more negative.

questions.stem: What does the transcript suggest about how media framing works on audiences?

options.text: The identical clip proves the minister's conduct was itself the cause of the difference
options.misconception: blames the minister's conduct for a difference produced by framing

options.text: The surrounding commentary shaped what audiences concluded from the same material
The two groups must have differed in education and therefore in their answers
options.misconception: invents a group difference the transcript never mentions

options.text: The channel's criticism shows that audiences ignore the evidence they are shown
options.misconception: assumes audiences reject the material they are shown

questions.explanation: Because the clip was identical, the difference in responses comes from the surrounding commentary rather than the material or the groups' backgrounds. Framing helps audiences interpret what they see.
questions.hint: Only the surrounding comment differed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why rules and practice can diverge in one country.
questions.stem: Explain why the same country can have democratic institutions on paper and an authoritarian regime in practice, and name two features that reveal the difference.

answer.exemplar: A system sets out the durable rules for who may compete, decide and be held accountable, while a regime describes the pattern of power actually practised within those rules. Institutions can therefore be copied faithfully in law and hollowed out in practice. Two revealing features are whether election outcomes are respected when they go against the government, and whether courts and the press can act on the executive without being punished. Where results are ignored or critics are sanctioned, the formal system does not describe the regime in being.

questions.explanation: Systems set out formal rules while regimes describe power as practised, so institutions can be copied in law and hollowed out in practice. Whether results are honoured and critics punished reveal the difference.
questions.hint: Look at how outcomes and critics are treated.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a characteristic of authoritarian rule in a profile.

stimulus.body: The profile records that opposition parties may hold meetings, but any meeting they hold is attended by officials who take notes, and no opposition announcement has appeared in the state broadcaster's news bulletins for the past two years. Voter turnout at the last election was 61 per cent.

questions.stem: Based on the profile, which feature of authoritarian rule is clearest here?

options.text: The absence of any legal opposition parties at all
options.misconception: overstates the facts by denying that opposition parties exist

options.text: The unusually high level of voter turnout at the last election
options.misconception: treats turnout as evidence of an authoritarian feature

options.text: The presence of permitted opposition that cannot reach the public
The failure of the opposition to win seats in the election
options.misconception: reads an electoral result as a marker of authoritarian practice

questions.explanation: Opposition is allowed to exist but is fenced in: notes are taken and its messages never reach the state broadcaster, which removes its ability to shape opinion. High turnout does not offset that.
questions.hint: Ask whether opposition can communicate freely.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish cross-sectional association from a trend.
questions.stem: A survey chart plots political interest against age and shows a single downward line. What does the chart support, and what does it not?

options.text: It shows that older citizens have no political interest whatsoever today
options.misconception: reads a group average as proof that no older citizen is interested

options.text: It shows that political interest among older citizens must be rising over time
options.misconception: mistakes a comparison between age groups for a change over time

options.text: It shows that the trend has been measured consistently over a long period
options.misconception: assumes a single chart establishes long-term measurement consistency

options.text: It shows a cross-sectional association that cannot establish a trend over time

questions.explanation: A plot of interest against age compares groups at one moment, so it cannot show how interest changes over the years. It supports an association between age and interest, and no more.
questions.hint: A cross-section is not a time series.

questions.learningObjective: Identify behaviours that mark a participant culture.
questions.stem: Which combination of behaviours best indicates a participant culture rather than an observer culture?

options.text: Voting regularly, joining associations and organising with others on issues
Reading the news each morning and discussing politics with acquaintances
options.misconception: confuses regular attention with organised participation

options.text: Following elections online and sharing posts without joining any group
options.misconception: treats online sharing as equivalent to collective action

options.text: Occasionally attending a public meeting and reading the summary afterwards

questions.explanation: Participation means acting with others in the formal business of politics, so voting, joining and organising together mark a participant culture. Attention and sharing alone, however regular, remain observation.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a value can fail to settle a concrete choice.

stimulus.body: One respondent said that honesty in public life is the standard she judges every politician by, and that she nonetheless had never voted because none of the candidates on offer seemed honest enough. Another said she voted only for the candidate her employer approved of, while holding that election turnout is a civic duty.

questions.stem: What do the two statements together show about values and attitudes?

options.text: That values determine voting behaviour whenever they are clearly stated
options.misconception: assumes clear values always dictate concrete choices

options.text: That a value may set a standard without settling the choices it is applied to
That stated values are unreliable because both respondents acted against them
options.misconception: concludes that every inconsistent act makes a value unreliable

options.text: That only the second respondent's behaviour counts as political action
options.misconception: judges which behaviour counts without a stated principle

questions.explanation: Each respondent applies a value to a concrete situation and reaches a different choice, so a value sets a standard rather than dictating a decision. Departing from a standard is not evidence the standard is unreliable.
questions.hint: Standards guide choices without making them automatic.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare childhood and adult political socialisation.
questions.stem: Explain how political socialisation differs between a person who was socialised in childhood and one who was socialised as an adult, and state which differences matter for research.

answer.exemplar: Childhood socialisation occurs before a person has formed durable views, when attitudes are still fluid and learning is largely indirect through family and schooling, so the orientations absorbed are likely to persist and to be taken for granted. Adult socialisation is usually more deliberate and tied to a specific event or interest, so it tends to be more specific, more easily questioned and less stable. For research this matters because the sources, the depth of internalisation and the expected durability of the result all differ, so the two cases should not be pooled as if they were the same process.

questions.explanation: Childhood socialisation occurs while attitudes are fluid, so what is absorbed persists and is taken for granted. Adult socialisation is more deliberate and specific, so source, depth and durability differ.
questions.hint: Note the timing of learning and its durability.

options.misconception: assumes the survey limited pupils to one possible answer

options.misconception: dismisses the leading source on grounds of sample size without evidence

Teachers are the strongest source because schools reach every pupil on a schedule

questions.explanation: Parents are named most often, so within these three schools the family is the most frequently cited source for how pupils would decide. The survey establishes no more than that, and scheduling does not make teachers decisive.
questions.hint: Read the percentages before generalising.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of a single survey indicator.
questions.stem: Explain why measuring political culture with a single survey indicator is problematic, and state what a sound design would require.

answer.exemplar: A single indicator collapses a broad, layered construct into one answer, so it cannot distinguish how widely a value is held from how deeply it is internalised, and a country can score well on one question while being weak on another. A sound design needs multiple items that tap distinct dimensions, a clear definition of what is being measured, wording and timing held constant across places, and an acknowledgement that attitudes differ in depth, not only in direction. Without those, a chart of scores invites comparisons the instrument cannot support.

questions.explanation: One indicator flattens a layered construct and cannot show how deeply an attitude is held. A sound design needs several items across dimensions, constant wording and timing, and attention to depth as well as direction.
questions.hint: One question cannot cover a layered construct.

options.misconception: invents a survey instrument difference not recorded anywhere

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how framing, not exposure, carries the socialising effect.
questions.stem: Explain how television news can socialise citizens politically even when no election is approaching, and why the effect depends on framing rather than on exposure alone.

answer.exemplar: Television news arrives in most homes as part of the daily routine, so its recurring features, such as which institutions are consulted, which professions are trusted and which problems are treated as urgent, are absorbed across many ordinary evenings rather than in a single campaign. The influence depends on framing because the same event can be presented as a scandal, a failure or a warning, each of which teaches a different expectation about how power behaves. Exposure without framing teaches only that the subject exists.

questions.explanation: Daily news carries political lessons in what it routinely treats as credible and urgent, so framing is what shapes those lessons. Mere exposure without framing would teach only that the topic exists.
questions.hint: Framing teaches expectations, exposure only presence.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why stated values may not predict behaviour.
questions.stem: Explain why a survey that asks only for stated values may give a misleading picture of how people will actually behave politically.

answer.exemplar: Stated values are what respondents are willing to report, and reporting is shaped by social expectations, by the demand for consistency and by a wish to appear principled, so the answer and the action can diverge. Some respondents also hold a value in general terms without attaching it to the specific choice in front of them, and will vote against a party they think violates it. Values are therefore best treated as one input alongside behaviour, not as a prediction of it.

questions.explanation: Stated values are filtered by what respondents are willing to report and may not attach to a concrete choice, so they can diverge from behaviour. Values are one input into explanation, not a forecast of action.
questions.hint: Asking is not the same as doing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how authoritarian rule is sustained with active civil society.
questions.stem: Describe how authoritarian rule is typically sustained in a state with an active civil society, and explain why repression alone is rarely the whole story.

answer.exemplar: Authoritarian rule is usually sustained by a mixture of inducement and constraint. Officials grant favourable treatment to compliant organisations, subsidise friendly media and permit some harmless assembly, which secures cooperation without visible repression and makes challengers reluctant to risk privileged access. At the same time, legal and extralegal constraints are applied to the most threatening activities. Repression alone is rarely sufficient because it is costly, it generates international attention and it can galvanise otherwise passive groups, whereas a system with legitimate channels and material rewards produces quieter compliance.

questions.explanation: Authoritarian rule typically combines inducements that buy cooperation with constraints that target threats, because pure repression is costly and can rally opposition. Privileged access and material rewards secure quieter compliance.
questions.hint: Ask what compliance costs and what it buys.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why identifying the agent matters in research.
questions.stem: Explain why it matters for research to identify which agent exercised a given influence, and give two reasons.

answer.exemplar: Identifying the agent tells the researcher what kind of mechanism is operating. If a family shapes a child's view, the mechanism is transmission within a household, which is durable, hard to contest and usually invisible to the child; if a teacher or a peer shapes it, the mechanism is instruction or conformity, which is more explicit and more open to challenge. The distinction also matters for comparison, because a country with strong schools and a country with strong families are likely to produce different political profiles, and a claim about one should not be generalised to the other.

questions.explanation: Different agents work through different mechanisms, household transmission being durable and implicit while teaching and peer pressure are explicit and contestable. Identifying the agent prevents generalising across contexts.
questions.hint: Name the mechanism, not just the source.

options.misconception: treats a coincidence as the cause of the trust figures

options.text: Schools are irrelevant to political learning wherever television is widely used
options.misconception: assumes one learning source excludes the other

options.text: Trust in journalists has no connection with how citizens learn about politics
options.misconception: denies any relationship between the two measured series

questions.explanation: In five of six countries where television is the main source, reported trust in journalists is lowest, which supports a link between reliance and scepticism. The figures are associative and schools remain a source.
questions.hint: Note the pattern across countries, not one case.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Judge a democracy claim from institutional and behavioural evidence.
questions.stem: Which judgement best fits the evidence that a country has competitive elections but no transfer of power has ever occurred?

options.text: The country must be democratic because the elections themselves are competitive
options.misconception: treats competitive elections as decisive evidence of a democratic regime

options.text: The country has no political system because elections are contested
options.misconception: assumes the existence of elections rules out having a political system

options.text: The country's constitution must be rewritten before it can be classified
options.misconception: prescribes constitutional change instead of drawing a classification

options.text: Competitive elections form part of the system, while the absence of turnover points to the regime

questions.explanation: Competitive elections describe how the system allocates power, while the absence of turnover describes the regime in operation. The two findings belong to different levels of analysis and are compatible.
questions.hint: Put each piece of evidence at the right level.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the feature that most limits accountability.
questions.stem: Which feature most directly limits the ability of citizens to hold an authoritarian government accountable?

options.text: The absence of an independent judiciary that can rule against the executive
The existence of a written constitution that names rights in general terms
options.misconception: treats written rights on paper as effective constraint

options.text: The presence of elections at regular intervals, whatever the outcome
options.misconception: assumes regular elections create accountability regardless of the outcome

options.text: The size of the legislature, provided it meets on a fixed schedule
options.misconception: confuses institutional size with actual capacity to check power

questions.explanation: Accountability requires a body able to rule against the executive and have the ruling stick, so an independent judiciary does the work here. Written rights, elections and a large legislature can exist without constraining power.
questions.hint: Ask what can actually rule against the government.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a generational trust and turnout comparison.

stimulus.body: The report compares the same three questions across five countries and reports the answers of the oldest and youngest age groups side by side. It notes that in every country the youngest group reported less trust in established institutions than the oldest, and that the gap was widest in the country with the lowest overall turnout.

questions.stem: According to the extract, which relationship does the data support?

options.text: Lower trust among younger cohorts accompanies lower participation in that country
options.misconception: infers a causal link between trust levels and turnout in one country

options.text: The widest generational gap in trust occurs in the country with the lowest turnout
The youngest cohort in every country is shown to have the strongest political values
options.misconception: treats lower institutional trust as evidence of strong political values

options.text: Older respondents in every country report higher participation than younger ones
options.misconception: assumes reported trust levels reveal actual participation rates

questions.explanation: The extract records that the widest trust gap occurs in the country with the lowest turnout, supporting an association between distrust and weaker participation. The measures are separate, so no cause is established.
questions.hint: Match the country with the widest gap.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why rising attention need not raise participation.
questions.stem: Explain why a sharp rise in political attention need not produce a rise in political participation, and what would have to change for participation to follow.

answer.exemplar: Attention can be raised cheaply by events, by alarming coverage and by social media discussion, none of which asks anything of the reader beyond looking. Participation asks for time, often money, and sometimes exposure to a risk of losing a job or a friendship, and those costs are set by institutions rather than by information. For participation to follow, the costs of acting would have to fall, which typically requires time at work, protection against retaliation, accessible venues and organisations that help people act, as well as the removal of legal and practical barriers.

questions.explanation: Attention can be stimulated at almost no cost, whereas participation demands time, money and sometimes risk, and those costs are set by institutions. Participation follows only if the costs of acting fall.
questions.hint: Attention is cheap; acting has a price.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a gap between principle and personal acceptance.

stimulus.body: The chart plots the share of adults who say political decisions should reflect the majority view against the share who say they personally accept the decision once made. In four of the six countries the first figure exceeds 80 per cent, while the second sits between 42 and 61 per cent.

questions.stem: What does the chart note suggest about the relationship between the two views?

options.text: Both views measure the same idea, so the gap between them is a recording error
options.misconception: assumes the two figures must be measuring the same thing

options.text: The low acceptance figure means most respondents reject majority rule itself
options.misconception: reads weak acceptance of outcomes as rejection of the principle

options.text: Support for majority rule in principle exceeds acceptance of particular outcomes
The gap between the two views disappears once turnout is taken into account
options.misconception: invents a turnout correction the chart never mentions

questions.explanation: In every country shown, support for deciding by majority exceeds the share who accept whatever is decided, so many endorse the principle in general while accepting specific outcomes less readily. The figures measure different things.
questions.hint: Compare principle with personal acceptance.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the finding that the earliest political memory is familial.
questions.stem: Which statement best fits a chart showing that a person's earliest political memory is typically a family occasion?

options.text: It proves that every later political view must resemble the family's view
options.misconception: treats an early starting point as permanent political uniformity

options.text: It shows that the family is the only agent that matters for political learning
options.misconception: excludes other agents because the earliest one is identified

options.text: It confirms that early memories have no lasting effect on adult politics
options.misconception: denies lasting influence while the chart points to its importance

options.text: The family enters political learning early, though later agents can still reshape it

questions.explanation: The finding identifies where political learning typically begins, making the family an early and important agent, but it does not show that later agents leave no mark. Neither permanence nor irrelevance is established.
questions.hint: Early start does not mean fixed outcome.
